Surficial and Quaternary Deposits The Quaternary deposits consist of alluvium, terrace deposits, blanket sands, beach sands, and dune deposits. Their thickness varies considerably, reaching up to 300 feet (ft) within major stream valleys but thinning to 100 ft or less elsewhere. These deposits can locally provide fresh water, particularly in coastal areas east of San Juan, where surficial lenses of freshwater float above denser salt water. However, these freshwater bodies are typically thin (≤100 ft), restricting development to small domestic supplies (Gómez-Gómez 1987). Stratigraphic Framework • Aymamón Limestone: In this area, the unit contains mostly salt water due to its proximity to the coast and influence from seawater intrusion (Gómez-Gómez 1987). • Aguada Limestone: In the SJMA, this formation contains a higher proportion of sand and clay compared to its occurrence in the western North Coast Province. It intercalates with chalky beds of the Cibao Formation and becomes indistinguishable from it about 0.5 miles east of the Río de la Plata (~15 km west of San Juan). • Cibao Formation: Composed mainly of limestone, sand, and clay. In this area, it intercalates and grades laterally eastward with the Mucarabones Sand. Importantly, it is the principal freshwater-bearing unit in the SJMA, not because of high yields, but because it is the thickest unit (~200 ft) containing fresh water (Giusti 1978; Gómez- Gómez 1987). • Mucarabones Sand: Characterized by cross-bedded, grayish-orange to yellow, fine- to medium-grained sand. Near the base, it becomes coarser, containing gravel and lenses of greenish-gray sandy clay. The unit extends from Río Grande de Manatí to San Juan and reaches its maximum thickness (~300 ft) between Río de la Plata and Río Bayamón (~10 km west of San Juan). Few wells draw exclusively from this unit, leaving its full freshwater supply potential uncertain (Rodríguez-Martínez 1995). Hydrostratigraphic Units of the North Coast Limestone Aquifer System Hydrogeologic investigations (Giusti 1978; Gómez-Gómez 1987; Rodríguez-Martínez 1995) show that the SJMA forms part of the North Coast Limestone aquifer system, which consists of three major hydrostratigraphic units: • Upper Aquifer: Composed primarily of the Aymamón Limestone and the Aguada Limestone and locally includes the upper Cibao Formation and surficial alluvium. It contains water under water-table conditions, except in coastal areas where fine-grained sediments locally confine the system. A saltwater zone underlies the freshwater zone in the coastal region. The Aymamón Limestone is the most permeable unit, with hydraulic conductivities ranging from 57 to 570 ft/d, although values diminish with depth. Minor water-bearing units in the SJMA show transmissivity values of 200–500 ft²/d. • Middle Confining Unit: Consists of low-permeability rocks, including the upper Cibao Formation, Quebrada Arenas Limestone, Río Indio Limestone, and mudstone.
